questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer:
Money. I had to be sure, that I would not bankrupt myself on an exchange. Here the Erasmus grant was paramount. 
Likewise, the academics. I study Theatre and Performance, and the only University in Europe that made sense for me, was then Berlin. Especially since they offer Dance Studies, which we don't have in Denmark.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer:
There has been ups and downs. I'm not good with bureaucracy, and trying to figure out all the documents to be filled out before- during-, and after the exchange was mentally super taxing for me, and gave rise to a lot of stress. I realise – and appreciate – the measures that have been taken to make it as comprehensive as possible for the student, but I still don't understand how I managed to do it all. And as I'm writing this, I am not done yet. 

And then there are personal matters as well: Subletting my apartment turned into chaos, which was also draining. 

The experiences I've gotten at my exchange destination have been life changing, however, and I've definitely grown!

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Honestly, everything is such a blur, because a lot of things happened at the same time, but I remember it being all right.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: There were meet-ups (meet 'n' greet) which were super helpful, campus tours which was also nice, very fruitful. An arranged meeting with my faculty Erasmus Coordinator was worth its weight in gold.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: The only comment is that I wish that we were given written information about the Campus Management anmeldung, because that confused me profoundly, seeing as it is miles apart from how we do things at UCPH. I tried to take notes at the oral 'how-to' presentation, but still felt at a loss when I actually had to do it.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: I ended up paying a lot, in order to have a secured housing situation (Neon Wood). Right off the bat, I wouldn't recommend it, because it was too expensive. I guess it's a question of how much you're willing to pay for (an early) peace of mind. I had gotten quite scared of the "Berlin is in a housing crisis" narrative, which is true, but my fear might have gotten out of proportions.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer:
I would search on the outskirts of the city (but not further out than 40-ish minutes from the city). Try finding a map of the U-bahns and S-bahns and look around those areas. Don't be afraid of subletting/sharing with others! Where you decide to live ultimately depends on what you want to have easiest access to (uni or the city). 
If I were to do this again, I could imagine searching for sublets in Steglitz, especially if you're going in the summer.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer:
I had heard/heard some not-so-great stories about the housing offered by FU. One had bedbugs. Another saw cockroaches in the office rooms. A third had a room that straight up looked like a little jail cell, facing a busy road. 

And also the two locations offered were too far away from the city for me.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: It is built very differently than at my home university (UCPH), and even though I was at an info lecture about how to do it, when I then actually sat down with it, I was thoroughly confused.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer:
Well, I guess I didn't make it easy for myself, since I took part in MA courses even though I'm a BA. That means that I couldn't register on Campus Management, since those courses weren't available to me. This resulted in a lot of back and forth e-mailing with several professors. It was worth it though!! Without a doubt. 
Process:
1. Look at the course catalogue and figure out what courses you want to attend
2. (Only relevant for Erasmus students) Figure out how many ECTS credits the courses give you. This was unnecessarily difficult. 
3. Do the ECTS credit math, and try to make it match your interests + requirements from home
4. Apply for those courses on Campus Management if they are there (as said, MA courses are not visible for BA students)
4.1 If they are not there, write the professor
4.2 If you have not gotten your immatrikulationsnummer, write the professor. 

Actually, during this whole process, the most common answer to my questions was, "write to the professor".

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer:
I was super lucky to be sitting in the student café, when I did the application. The other students who knew the system were super helpful. 

The big auditorium presentation was also helpful to some extend. 

My Erasmus coordinator was also very nice with helping me build a good schedule.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I got all of the classes I wished, so I would say quite succesful. Though I wouldn't recommend bending the structure too much, like I did. As an Erasmus student you have the option do to extra work for extra credits. I did this, in order to take some classes that interested me, but would leave me with not enough credits. Dance Studies offered a structure for the ideal MA course of study, and I should have followed that one.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Don't be afraid to talk to the other students!! And be in the student café(s) as much as possible. There's a lot of help to be found there. At least that was my experience.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I have no comments, I found it great.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: Both

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: I did three on the BA level and three on the MA level

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer:
I have come to appreciate UCPH teaching quite a lot. FU's style of teaching (when it comes to classroom teaching and not Übungskurse) is very much discussion based, meaning that you show up, have a discussion, and then leave. I prefer the UCPH model where the teacher interprets the text(s) of the day, naming its most important points, why we have read it etc. and THEN we go into a discussion. I find this to provide a better starting point for meaningful discussions than "just" jumping right in. 
   Though it's difficult to put to words, I find UCPH's teaching more structured which fits me better. 

However! The practical courses (Übungskurse) that FU offers, were beyond amazing. I really miss more practical work at UCPH.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer: "Writing Dance on Film", "Introduction to Critical Dance Studies", "Rhythm & Movement", ""The personal is political" – Micropolitics in Dance and Performance", "Listening Together" and "Erkunden/Entwerfen/Probieren"

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Practical courses! Without a doubt. Simply because we don't have them at UCPH. But keep the ECTS credits in mind – there's a puzzle that has to come together. And if I may, anything that Professor Lindsey Drury teaches, I would highly recommend. She is a powerhouse of an academic/artist.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: I didn't realise that you had to rent cleaning supplies at the place where I stayed. I ended up renting through UniRents. And that no pillow/duvet was supplied, which I then had to buy.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Food is way less expensive in Germany. The price for washing clothes was also higher than expected.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer:
Hochschulsport, as they are called, have an extensive variety of courses that they offer. 

They have, however, not matched the FU course registration timeline. If you apply for a sport course, and then it doesn't fit your academic schedule, well tough luck. You can de-register but you can't get your money back. And if you wait too long, you risk the class getting fully booked.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: These are Erasmus coordinated and might not count then, but we were offered a tour of the Bundestag, a boat tour of Berlin and a Festival of Lights quiz (that one I did and it was awesome)

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Well, as a theatre/dance student I would say explore the cultural scene. Enjoy the richness of the Berlin stage so long it lasts (they are experiencing budget cuts). Try to find some nice bars/cafés to explore different Kiez-vibes. Hochschulsport was great, I met friends there, and it's cheap.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: I haven't been good enough at taking advantage of the D-Semesterticket. Take some (day) trips to Potsdam, Görlitz and the like. And go to Flohmarkten!

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Quite easy. It's not that different from Denmark, and I've been to Berlin before.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Get involved in student initiatives. I choose to work at the student café, and it was wonderful.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: None, really.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: Berliners have a quite laid-back attitude. They're not really in a hurry.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1. Prepare for way less structure than at UCPH. You have much more influence at FU. 
2. Prepare for quite a lot of active participation and obligatory attendance. 
3. Just when you feel that now you know the city, it'll be time for you to leave. Time flies. Therefore, - do that thing that you wanted to, talk to that person that you find cool, ask that friend that you do something together. Learn as you go.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: FU can seem unstructured and chaotic at first, but you will get it. Don't be afraid to do what is "expected" or follow a quite straight forward path, - it's not boring. It will (hopefully) provide you with more time and calm.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer:
Two things: The people I met, and the courses at Critical Dance Studies. 
I was so incredibly, unfathomably lucky with the people I got to study with, and being allowed to take MA courses and really focus on dance which is my great passion, was fantastic.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Seeking revised pre-approvals, getting new Online Learning Agreements etc. Basically the bureaucracy. I even messed up, and am still dealing with it now as I am writing this.

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: No:)

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
